Among LLM-based baselines, it improves recovery by at least 54.91% while using at most 17.4% of the strongest competitor's mean search time. On 122 BlackBox datasets, DIGEST achieves the highest accuracy while maintaining a moderate model complexity.

Machine Learning.title: Align, Then Adapt: Few-Shot fMRI Visual Reconstruction For New Subjects
Machine Learning.summary: Reconstructing visual images from fMRI data is a central but challenging problem in neuroscience. Despite recent progress, current methods fall short when data and computation are limited-precisely the conditions under which this task is most critical. We introduce Adapter Alignment, a staged, architecture-agnostic training procedure for adapting a pre-trained reconstruction model to a new subject with little data. Rather than letting a shared representation space emerge implicitly, lightweight subject-specific adapters are first explicitly aligned to a pre-trained reference subject on a small set of shared calibration images, and the full pipeline is then fine-tuned while preserving this alignment. The resulting representations not only place different subjects in a shared space but also align them semantically. Our results demonstrate significant gains in low-data regimes, improving reconstruction metrics by up to 8%, and pre-diffusion retrieval shows that these gains reflect additional image-specific information in the fMRI embeddings rather than the generative prior. We also propose a coverage-based algorithm to select representative calibration images. Using both techniques together, we surpass baseline models fine-tuned with one hour of data using only 24 minutes of subject-specific data. The procedure is effective across architectures, reference subjects, and datasets, including adapting 3T subjects to a 7T reference.

Machine Learning.title: Stable Dimensionality Reduction via Isometric Centroid-Encoder
Machine Learning.summary: Many supervised dimensionality reduction methods promote intra-class compactness and inter-class separation but do not explicitly constrain class geometry, leading to variability in the relative arrangement of classes across independent runs. Such variability limits the reproducibility and interpretability of low-dimensional embeddings. We propose the Isometric Centroid-Encoder (ICE), a supervised dimensionality reduction framework in which class centroids are learned directly in the latent space while preserving a prescribed pairwise class-centroid geometry. Unlike existing centroid- or prototype-based methods that primarily encourage intra-class compactness, ICE explicitly regularizes the relative arrangement of latent class centroids. Unlike multidimensional scaling and many metric-learning approaches that preserve sample-level relationships, ICE operates on class centroids, preserving inter-class geometry without requiring large numbers of sample-pair or triplet constraints. We further show that the intrinsic dimensionality required to represent the centroid-distance configuration of $M$ classes is at most $M-1$, explaining the observed saturation of distance-preservation measures as the latent dimensionality increases. To quantify embedding reproducibility, we introduce the Centroid Neighborhood Stability (CNS) metric, which measures the consistency of class-level neighborhood topology across independent runs and complements existing embedding quality measures. Experiments on image and biological datasets demonstrate that ICE produces stable embeddings with improved preservation of class-centroid geometry while remaining computationally efficient. Additional analyses of optimization dynamics, sensitivity, and preprocessing further provide practical insights into latent dimensionality and explicit geometry modeling for supervised dimensionality reduction.

Machine Learning.title: MAGNET: Manifold-Aware Graph Diffusion Network for Connectome Generation
Machine Learning.summary: Functional brain connectome represents neural connectivity as a matrix of pairwise interactions between brain regions. Generation of functional connectomes is not only a question of validity; rather, having satisfied the constraints on the correlation matrix, the next step is to recover the class-conditional geometry buried under coarse labels. We propose MAGNET, a Manifold-Aware Graph Diffusion Network which uses a normalized-Cholesky representation of the manifold of correlation matrices that guarantees validity. MAGNET lifts noisy latent states into ROI-level region tokens and performs denoising with a relational inductive bias over brain atlas regions. To deal with structural problems induced by coarse labels, MAGNET employs class-anchored conditioning, amortized structural bridge, and relevance-preserving corruption. Across ABIDE, ADNI, and OASIS-3, MAGNET consistently achieves favorable results compared to previous manifold-aware approaches, demonstrating improvements of 7-21% in class-conditional fidelity ($α,β$-F1) across three cohorts and better sampling efficiency. Moreover, while training only with strict binary labels, MAGNET is capable of maintaining clinical heterogeneity through fine substructure of the connectomes in a zero-shot setting, improving subclass covariance alignment ($λ$-MSE) by over 30%. These results suggest that geometric validity is a necessary but insufficient condition for clinical utility in connectome synthesis. Moreover, efforts in making the diffusion denoising class-conditional manifold aware finds utility beyond the highly curved brain connectome generation as this is a critical problem in various general settings. The code repository can be found at https://github.com/protyayofficial/MAGNET.

Machine Learning.title: Numina Fuse: Interactive Autoformalization in Lean 4
Machine Learning.summary: Numina Fuse is an agent-native application for formalizing mathematics in Lean 4. Since Lean can compile while not representing its intended informal meaning, and agents now write Lean faster than people can read it, we built Fuse around human supervision of agent work. A user works with an AI orchestrator on a Lean project and supervises it through views of the blueprint, the dependency graph, and the Lean code, while the backend keeps the project's derived state and runs agents for hours without the user present. We describe the development of Fuse throughout 2026, as it moved from a prescribed pipeline of agents paced by human review to an orchestrator that dispatches specialists, provers, and parallel children on its own. We designed for this shift, keeping project state, tooling, and interface design separate from orchestration so that agents could take over more of the work as models improved. We report Fuse's use in a formalization of the three-dimensional Kakeya conjecture and a study of prover models. We close with lessons for the next generation of autoformalization systems. Fuse Desktop, an open-source local version, is available at https://github.com/project-numina/fuse-desktop.

Machine Learning.title: Vib2ECG: A Co-Located Chest-Lead SCG-ECG Dataset and Benchmark for ECG Reconstruction
Machine Learning.summary: Twelve-lead electrocardiography (ECG) is essential for cardiovascular diagnosis, but its long-term acquisition in daily life is constrained by complex and costly hardware. Recent efforts have explored reconstructing ECG from low-cost cardiac vibrational signals such as seismocardiography (SCG), with prior studies primarily focusing on limb leads, while clinical diagnosis requires multi-lead ECG, including chest leads. In this work, we propose Vib2ECG, a dataset of synchronized, co-located ECG and chest-wall vibration recordings, which includes complete twelve-lead ECGs and vibrational signals acquired by inertial measurement units (IMUs) at the six standard precordial electrode sites (V1-V6) from 17 subjects. Based on this dataset, we also provide a benchmark. Experimental results demonstrate the feasibility of reconstructing electrical cardiac signals at variable locations from vibrational signals using a lightweight 364K-parameter U-Net. Furthermore, we observe a hallucination phenomenon in the model, where ECG waveforms are generated in regions where no corresponding electrical activity is present. We analyze the causes of this phenomenon and propose potential directions for mitigation. This study demonstrates the feasibility of mobile-device-friendly ECG monitoring through chest-lead ECG prediction from low-cost vibrational signals acquired using IMU sensors. It expands the application of cardiac vibrational signals and provides new insights into the spatial relationship between cardiac electrical and mechanical activities with spatial location variation.
Machine Learning.comment: Added ethics approval information and clarified the description of co-located SCG-ECG acquisition at V1-V6

Machine Learning.title: Representation-Aligned Auxiliary Supervision for Language Model Adaptation
Machine Learning.summary: Language models exhibit strong reasoning capabilities, yet adapting them to structured domains remains challenging and can yield inconsistent outcomes. We identify representation compatibility, the extent to which a model effectively processes a representation for a structured task, as a key factor in adaptation. We study this in chess, which provides a controlled testbed with precise semantics, computable optimal actions, and multiple state representations, including a symbolic encoding (FEN) and a spatial format (ASCII). We find that models often process semantically equivalent inputs substantially differently, affecting both learning and generalization. Building on this observation, we propose representation-aligned auxiliary supervision, which uses environment-derived tasks expressed in compatible representations to improve adaptation to structured domains. Across models and representations, auxiliary supervision consistently improves optimal-move prediction relative to target-only training under identical target data. Tasks that expose environment dynamics provide larger and most consistent gains than surface-level or static supervision, while remaining competitive with substantially increasing the amount of target-task data. Moreover, ASCII-trained models transfer more effectively to FEN than FEN-trained models do to ASCII, even surpassing the FEN target-only baseline on FEN evaluation. The gains also extend beyond optimal-move prediction to open-ended, factually grounded commentary generation. Overall, our results show that auxiliary supervision in model-compatible representations can enable effective adaptation in structured domains.

Machine Learning.title: Software Engineering LLMs: Why We Need Them and How Software Engineering Helps Build Them
Machine Learning.summary: Software engineering (SE) expertise can shape how coding large language models (LLMs) are trained and which engineering capabilities they acquire. We examine this role through an industrial case study of capability-focused training for a 92B-parameter coding LLM serving more than 100,000 developers. We demonstrate how established SE knowledge can guide the selection of engineering capabilities, the construction of verifiable training data, and the evaluation of model improvements. To target repository-level refactoring, we developed RefactorForge, a pipeline that combines refactoring knowledge, established SE tools, and verification techniques to construct training data. Across 306 Python repositories, RefactorForge generated 5,704 executable tasks and retained 4,572 verified teacher trajectories totaling 72.51 million tokens. Incremental supervised fine-tuning on these trajectories, accounting for 0.46% of the preceding coding mixture's tokens, improved RefactorBench performance by 18.00 percentage points and SWE-Bench ProMax performance by 7.06 points. Under OpenCode, these improvements extended to SWE issue resolution, with gains of 4.97 points on SWE-Bench Verified and 1.23 points on SWE-Bench Pro. Improvements also persisted across other coding-agent harnesses, while greenfield repository generation showed mixed results. We report lessons from constructing capability-focused training data and evaluating its effects across engineering workloads. Building on this industrial experience, we propose a research agenda for expanding SE's role in transforming coding LLMs into SE LLMs: incorporating SE knowledge into model training, applying engineering methods to model development and maintenance, and systematically defining the engineering capabilities these models should acquire.

Machine Learning.title: Ranking Is Not Deciding: Benchmark Shortcuts and Operating-Point Collapse in Query-Time RAG Poisoning Defenses
Machine Learning.summary: Query-time filters that screen each retrieved document before it reaches the generator are the dominant published defense against retrieval-augmented generation poisoning, and they report near-perfect detection on domain benchmarks. We show that this performance is predicted by how the poison set was built rather than by what the filter reads: removing a single construction cue destroys the deployed decision before it destroys the ranking. Two label-free statistics of a poison set and its clean corpus profile the cue: containment, how often the target question appears verbatim in the poison, and length overlap. PoisonedRAG's released code prepends the target question to every inserted passage. Of the 21 published defense evaluations we survey, 8 verifiably run poison built this way and 5 substitute a length cue; separately, 12 report no false-positive rate at the operating point they deploy. Deleting only that prefix from the attack authors' own passages (0.93 still retrieved for their target) takes RAGuard, a published content filter we re-implement, from AUROC 0.953 to 0.758 and its miss rate from 0.191 to 0.763. Across four corpora, four attack families and ten per-document defenses on one shared candidate set, the profile predicts where detection saturates. Padding medical poison to clean length with word-shuffled filler that carries no content takes TrustRAG's set-level stage from a miss rate of 0.000 to 0.827, and one learned scorer of ours from 0.000 to 0.986 (0.321 at a matched 5% false-positive rate) while its AUROC holds at 0.953. The ranking survives; the decision does not. A defense-aware attacker defeats our own scorer, so we claim no defense. A detection result is evidence only when it is reported with its poison set's construction profile and the false-positive rate at the threshold actually deployed; we release the script that computes the profile.

Machine Learning.title: PENEX: AdaBoost-Inspired Neural Network Regularization
Machine Learning.summary: AdaBoost sequentially fits so-called weak learners to minimize an exponential loss, which penalizes misclassified data points more severely than other loss functions like cross-entropy. Paradoxically, AdaBoost generalizes well in practice as the number of weak learners grows. In the present work, we introduce Penalized Exponential Loss (PENEX), a new formulation of the multi-class exponential loss that is theoretically grounded and, in contrast to the existing formulation, amenable to optimization via first-order methods, making it a practical objective for training neural networks. We demonstrate that PENEX effectively increases margins of data points, which can be translated into a generalization bound. Empirically, across computer vision and language tasks, PENEX improves neural network generalization in low-data regimes, matching and in some settings outperforming established regularizers at comparable computational cost. Our results highlight the potential of the exponential loss beyond its application in AdaBoost.

Machine Learning.title: Explainable GeoAI for urban wildfire structure loss: vegetation and built environment in the 2025 Palisades Fire
Machine Learning.summary: Urban wildfire resilience depends on interactions among built form, vegetation condition, and extreme fire weather, yet city-scale risk models often overlook whether predictive skill transfers across neighborhoods. We developed a spatially validated GeoAI workflow for the January 2025 Palisades Fire, linking 12,081 CAL FIRE damage inspections to pre-fire Sentinel-2 vegetation indices, Landsat surface temperature, LANDFIRE fuels, terrain, and OpenStreetMap buildings and roads. Among 9,883 inspected residential structures, 5,566 were destroyed. Random cross-validation yielded ROC-AUC 0.92 for the integrated XGBoost model, but 1 km spatial block validation reduced performance to 0.75; logistic regression performed similarly and was better calibrated. Building count within 100 m was the strongest predictor, with destruction odds increasing 4.12-fold per standard deviation. Vegetation moisture and greenness showed opposing conditional associations: NDMI at 100-300 m was protective (OR 0.52), whereas NDVI at 30-100 m was positively associated with destruction after accounting for moisture (OR 1.74). Predictive information was concentrated at the 100-300 m neighborhood scale. A separate post-fire track mapped burn severity and vegetation recovery without leakage. The results support neighborhood-scale susceptibility screening, moisture-aware vegetation management, and spatial block validation as a minimum standard for single-event urban wildfire modeling.
Machine Learning.comment: 20 pages, 13 figures, 4 tables (original preprint). Published in Frontiers in Sustainability, Volume 7, Article 1975724 (2026). Published version: https://doi.org/10.3389/frsus.2026.1975724. Data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22061862. Code: https://github.com/MohammadrezaNarimaniUCDavis/Palisades_Urban_Wildfire_GeoAI

Machine Learning.title: When is early stopping beneficial under label noise? A phase diagram for kernel gradient flow
Machine Learning.summary: Early stopping is commonly used to prevent fitting label noise from degrading generalization. Does this mean that, when a positive fraction of the training labels is intrinsically unpredictable, the best test error must occur before interpolation? Experiments on a CIFAR10 classification task with randomly labeled examples motivate the opposite possibility: although fixed-feature and shallow models exhibit late-time deterioration of the test error, the need for early stopping essentially disappears in larger, deeper convolutional networks even after the random labels have all been classified correctly. We determine when late-time deterioration disappears entirely in a solvable setting. For kernel gradient flow on a synthetic noisy classification task, we derive sharp high-dimensional learning curves and obtain a phase diagram controlled by the balance between the linear kernel component that learns the shared relation between inputs and labels and the higher-order components that enable fitting the label noise. In one regime, generalization is optimized at finite time and early stopping is necessary. In another, generalization improves until interpolation, but the endpoint is suboptimal across kernels. At the boundary, the interpolating endpoint attains the lowest generalization error across the considered kernel family and all training times. Thus, even with extensive irreducible label noise, interpolation can outperform early stopping. The neural-network experiments leave open how learned representations acquire an analogous favorable geometry.

Machine Learning.title: Build, Don't Play: Self-Improving LLM Research Agents Develop a Hearthstone Battlegrounds AI That Rivals Top Players
Machine Learning.summary: Can LLM agents carry a hard real-world problem from raw data to a system that holds its own against people? We study this in Hearthstone Battlegrounds, an eight-player auto-battler with stochastic shops and battles, hidden information and nearly a thousand interacting cards. We present AutoTavern, a self-improving research system: specialised LLM research agents share a typed research memory, every claim passes verification gates, and live games close the loop, so the agents improve the simulator, opponents and policy and, from the same feedback, their own research process; a human sets goals and rules on ambiguous mechanics. In 20 days AutoTavern built TavernGym, the first faithful, full-content reproduction of the live game, and delivered 23 versions of TavernAgent, trained with PPO against opponents calibrated to real games. TavernAgent plays complete games on the live ladder by itself: its rating rose from 6,000 to about 15,000 and, on the public leaderboard's measure, its last 20 records average a placement of 1.60 with 80% first places, better than the server's ten highest-rated players on every statistic (2.34, 59%). TavernBench, 960 tasks in 40 scenarios, shows that the system the agents built is the strongest player: TavernAgent answers 91% of the play tasks against at most 63% for frontier LLMs, and decides in 0.03 s where they need up to 26 s; within the second a live turn allows, it keeps 90% and no LLM more than 26%. LLM agents build far better than they play. We will open-source TavernBench and TavernGym at https://github.com/MCG-NJU/AutoTavern.
Machine Learning.comment: 20 pages, 8 figures, 15 tables. Code and benchmark: https://github.com/MCG-NJU/AutoTavern

Machine Learning.title: Approximate Universal Prediction under Interaction
Machine Learning.summary: Bayesian mixtures, and Solomonoff induction in particular, provide an idealized model of prediction learned by minimizing population log loss, and they underlie universal agents such as AIXI. An agent that plans with an approximation of such a predictor decides where that predictor is evaluated, and a planner can be drawn toward branches on which its model is optimistic. We study which approximation guarantees survive this feedback. For normalized finite-horizon causal mixtures, the transfer coefficient factors into a policy likelihood ratio and task evidence available before each prediction, so task rarity and action-branch rarity can compound. Within one fixed universal mixture, infinitely many computable environments admit excess prediction error of order $κη\,2^{K(μ)}$, where $η$ is the training KL budget and $κ$ measures policy coverage. This order is sharp, and for each target a computable predictor attains it at a suitable finite horizon, so computability alone does not remove the penalty. For bounded returns, value error is controlled by the probability of entering a poorly covered branch plus a square-root term in $η$. Both terms are necessary, and finite maximum coverage ratios are not required. Motivated by the mentor override of Golden Handcuffs, we derive margins for preserving deferral decisions and conditional KL budgets with an unavoidable inverse-history-probability penalty, and a counterexample separates agreement of deferral decisions from task-wise event avoidance. The guarantees apply to any predictor architecture that meets explicit population approximation and coverage conditions, which gives concrete targets for implementing idealized universal agents.

Machine Learning.title: FlexMARL: Graph-Driven Rollout-Training Co-Design for LLM-Based Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
Machine Learning.summary: Despite algorithm-level innovations for multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), the underlying infrastructure for large-scale MARL remains underexplored. Existing training frameworks primarily optimize for single-agent scenarios and fail to capture the graph-structured nature of MARL. This fundamental mismatch leads to three MARL-specific challenges: topology-induced rollout skew, critical path synchronization barriers, and dynamic training demand. To bridge this gap, we propose FlexMARL, a graph-driven rollout-training co-designed framework for large-scale LLM-based MARL. FlexMARL introduces the multi-agent execution graph (MEG) and materializes the intermediate representation as the MEG Store, which provides decentralized multi-table storage and serves as the data hub for system components. Built around the MEG Store, the Rollout Engine develops dependency parallel sampling with hierarchical load balancing, which reduces inference latency and balances intra-agent/inter-agent loads. The Joint Orchestrator exploits an agent-level asynchronous pipeline to mitigate the critical path synchronization barriers while maintaining consistency. The Training Engine achieves on-demand resource allocation by collectively managing training processes for individual agents. The training states of different agents are swapped via location-agnostic communication APIs. Empirical results on a production cluster demonstrate that FlexMARL achieves up to 7.3x speedup and improves hardware utilization by up to 5.6x compared to existing frameworks.

Machine Learning.title: Grounding on Request: Learning Modality Control in Vision-Language Models
Machine Learning.summary: When an image and its caption disagree, can a user reliably control which one a vision-language model (VLM) follows? Accuracy alone cannot answer this question, since a model might give the correct answer from parametric knowledge without following the requested evidence. We therefore evaluate modality grounding control through conflict-preserving counterfactual interventions. Specifically, Flip measures whether an initially correct answer follows an edit to the requested modality, while Stay measures whether it remains stable when the competing modality is edited. To learn this control, we build on neologism learning by introducing new words for visual and textual grounding, training only their embeddings while keeping the pretrained model fixed. We also introduce Counterfactual Twin-Margin (CTM) supervision, which uses paired interventions to teach how answer probabilities should change when the requested evidence changes. Across three VLMs on three existing benchmarks and our multi-attribute Ground-CF benchmark, we find that learned modality words improve control over natural-language instructions. Surprisingly, a single learned embedding per modality provides strong lightweight visual control and shows little average degradation on held-out values. LoRA remains strongest overall, although its visual advantage narrows under held-out evaluation. Moreover, counterfactual supervision improves control in several settings where standard supervision is weaker. Finally, we test our method on real-world news video and find that visual control improves when the relevant evidence is made easier to access. Overall, our results show that reliable modality control requires testing not only whether an answer is correct, but whether it continues to follow edits to the modality of choice.

Machine Learning.title: A Sentinel-2 benchmark dataset for deep-learning active-fire segmentation across 25 California wildfires, July 2020-August 2026
Machine Learning.summary: This article describes an open image dataset for developing and evaluating active-fire segmentation methods in satellite imagery. The dataset contains 2,148 image-mask pairs from 25 California wildfires, with acquisitions spanning July 2020 to August 2026. Each image is a 512x512-pixel, three-channel composite derived from Sentinel-2 Level-2A bands B12, B11 and B8A at 20 m spatial sampling. A fixed linear rendering is applied throughout the dataset. Corresponding masks distinguish background, SWIR-rule active fire and invalid observations. The masks were generated from shortwave-infrared brightness and near-infrared contrast, followed by constrained neighborhood growth. The release includes chip-level metadata and an incident-disjoint partition containing 18 training, three validation and four test fires. Among the image pairs, 841 contain active-fire labels; these labels occupy 0.0766% of all grid cells. A mask-blind analyst review covers 233 test chips and provides a separate assessment of the rule-generated labels at chip and connected-component levels. Reference training and evaluation code accompanies the data, including a ResNet-34 U-Net implementation with validation-based checkpoint and threshold selection. The archived images, masks, metadata and review annotations support research on rare-class segmentation, learning from algorithmic labels and transfer across fire incidents. The versioned dataset is deposited on Zenodo, with preparation and reuse software maintained in a public GitHub repository.
Machine Learning.comment: 13 pages, 9 figures, 5 tables. Published in Data in Brief (Elsevier), Volume 69, Article 113357 (2026). Data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22713948. Code: https://github.com/MohammadrezaNarimaniUCDavis/California_Sentinel2_Active_Fire_Dataset

Machine Learning.title: Sliding Networks: A Family of Residual Structures Preserving Feature Learning and Feature Diversity
Machine Learning.summary: Deep learning models tend to perform best at large widths and depths. The growing interest in scaling laws, especially in the language modeling domain, has motivated procedures for scaling up network widths and depths in order to preserve stability and computational efficiency of training dynamics. Existing depth-scaling approaches force a choice between retaining locally maximal \emph{feature learning} and preserving a form of \emph{feature diversity} in the residual stream arising from random differences between channels. We examine a \textit{joint scaling recipe} that preserves both. With residual width $N_\flat$, hidden width $N_\sharp$, and depth $L$, the key quantity is, by default, the limiting ratio $N_\flat/(N_\sharp L)\toα$, while correlated initialization (Half Copy) can partially relax the resulting shape constraints. Theory and residual-MLP experiments support convergence at fixed positive $α$ to an SDE limit with locally maximal feature learning. Hidden computations can then be redistributed between width and depth while preserving this limit, like turning melody into harmony and back. Language-model experiments nevertheless show performance differences under regrouping at fixed parameter count. These results distinguish approximating a limit (ODE or SDE) from scaling for better performance.

Machine Learning.title: EdgeDeID: A 0.6B Clinical De-identifier Trained Without Real Patient Data
Machine Learning.summary: De-identifying clinical notes with a hosted language model discloses the information the step is meant to protect. We present EdgeDeID, a 0.6B-parameter decoder-only de-identifier that runs locally and is trained without real patient text: three LLM teachers write synthetic notes, a single labeler re-annotates them into one convention, and the model learns to emit a typed XML schema of the identifiers it finds. On a 100-note synthetic in-domain benchmark with manually verified annotations it reaches 0.994 micro-F1 and leaves no missed identifier in 99% of notes, against 0.857 and 12% for the strongest of eight off-the-shelf systems. Quantized, it runs on CPU in 615 MB. Of three additions to supervised training, only a verifier adapter helps: it separates complete from incomplete outputs of other systems at 0.94 AUROC, whereas reinforcement learning with a recall-weighted reward and a rule-based post-processing layer leave in-domain results unchanged. On MIMIC ICU nursing notes F1 falls to 0.48. The errors follow two properties our synthetic notes lack, telegraphic style and low identifier density, and three hand-written in-context examples recover 0.08 F1 without annotated target data.
Machine Learning.comment: 18 pages, 2 figures. Under review at ACL Rolling Review (ARR). Code: https://github.com/BardiaKh/EdgeDeID ; models and data: https://huggingface.co/EdgeDeID

Machine Learning.title: Hessian-Similar Optimization with Capped Participation: Lower Bounds and Virtual Masters
Machine Learning.summary: What is the round complexity of Hessian-similar optimization when each round can contact at most $s$ of $m$ clients? Prior rates permit a free master or full participation and do not characterize strict caps. We count every one-vector query and reply. A hidden-client chain gives a lower bound for zero-respecting local algorithms with adaptive cohorts and random stopping: on strongly convex quadratics, the required rounds are $Ω((m/s)\sqrt{\min\{δ_a,\barδ/\sqrt m\}/μ}\,\log(1/ε))$ for $s\leq(m-2)/2$ in the high-accuracy, high-dissimilarity regime. Here $μ$ is strong convexity, while $δ_a$ and $\barδ$ bound anchor and average Hessian variation. To remove dependence on a poor anchor, virtual-master SVRS uses independent estimator and proximal cohorts and averages the proximal replies. With Catalyst, it reaches relative gap $ε$ in $\tilde O(m/s+(\sqrt{m/s}+m^{3/4}/s)\sqrt{\barδ/μ})$ expected rounds on quadratics with strongly convex clients, independent of $δ_a$. Combining this method with charged analyses of existing algorithms matches the lower bound's polynomial dependence for $s\leq\sqrt m$ and $s=Ω(m)$; the worst gap is $O(m^{1/8})$. A held-out 12-seed synthetic study finds fewer rounds than tuned SVRP in nine of ten dip-family incomplete-cohort cells, versus two of 30 other cells. The lower bounds concern zero-respecting algorithms and do not cover unrestricted messages.

Machine Learning.title: EEGBiFormer: Real-Time EEG Attention Classification via Hybrid CNN-Transformer with EEG-Informed Auditory Protocol Validation
Machine Learning.summary: Sustained attention is critical for academic performance, yet existing auditory support tools are static and not grounded in real-time neural evidence. This paper presents EEGBiFormer, a hybrid CNN-Transformer model for realtime binary classification of attention states, focus versus nonfocus, from 16-channel EEG signals. A custom analog front-end acquisition board was designed and built to collect a task-based EEG dataset. Before model training, spectral and connectivity analysis, using Power Spectral Density and Phase Locking Value, confirmed distinct neural signatures between attention states, providing physiological grounding for the classification approach. EEGBiFormer achieved 91.3 percent window-level validation accuracy with an F1 score of 94.5 percent, and 88.2 percent recording-level accuracy across 17 independent sessions. End-to-end system latency was measured below 100 ms, supporting real-time responsiveness. The trained model was further used to objectively rank auditory stimuli by focus-state confidence, yielding EEG-informed audio protocols. In a paired within-subject behavioral study with 37 participants, these protocols produced a statistically significant 20 percent improvement in composite attention scores over silent controls, with a medium-to-large effect size. This work demonstrates a complete pipeline from custom EEG hardware through neural signal analysis, deep learning classification, and evidence-based auditory protocol design.

Machine Learning.title: Provably Reliable Classifier Guidance via Cross-Entropy Control
Machine Learning.summary:
Classifier-guided diffusion models generate conditional samples by augmenting the reverse-time score with the gradient of the log-probability predicted by a probabilistic classifier. In practice, this classifier is usually obtained by minimizing an empirical loss function. While existing statistical theory guarantees good generalization performance when the sample size is sufficiently large, it remains unclear whether such training yields an effective guidance mechanism.
  We study this question in the context of cross-entropy loss, which is widely used for classifier training. Under mild smoothness assumptions on the classifier, we show that controlling the cross-entropy at each diffusion model step is sufficient to control the corresponding guidance error. In particular, probabilistic classifiers achieving conditional KL divergence $\varepsilon^2$ induce guidance vectors with mean squared error $\widetilde O(d \varepsilon )$, up to constant and logarithmic factors. Our result yields an upper bound on the sampling error of classifier-guided diffusion models and bears resemblance to a reverse log-Sobolev--type inequality. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first result that quantitatively links classifier training to guidance alignment in diffusion models, providing both a theoretical explanation for the empirical success of classifier guidance, and principled guidelines for selecting classifiers that induce effective guidance.

Machine Learning.title: Reactive Optimizers
Machine Learning.summary: We study a reactive optimizer that uses a pretrained language-model agent to inspect training dynamics and rewrite executable optimizer code during a single training run. The agent can change update rules and schedules for individual parameter groups, without optimizer-specific meta-training or memory transferred from other runs. We evaluate this approach, OPAL, on language modeling and image generation when a recipe has not been tuned for the target setting. Across the evaluated settings, it matches or improves on selected fixed recipes. Analysis of its decisions shows changes to learning-rate schedules, optimizer structure, numerical precision, and momentum. Controlled experiments also show adaptation to repeated data corruption and reduced overfitting. We report these behaviors together with the agent's computational cost and implementation requirements.
Machine Learning.comment: This document is a static version of our blog post. We recommend the original interactive version at https://xingjianbai.com/reactive-optimizers/. We release the code at https://github.com/xingjian-bai/opal

Machine Learning.title: Learning What to Share: Expert Specialization for Time-Series Forecasting
Machine Learning.summary: A central challenge in multivariate forecasting is deciding what to share across channels and where to specialize. Mixture-of-experts models offer flexible sharing, yet it remains unclear how much of their forecasting gains comes from added capacity or expert allocation. Through controlled comparisons across eleven datasets and three backbones, we show that informative channel assignments improve forecasting beyond matched shared capacity and random allocation. On frozen transformer backbones, persistent channel-specific mixtures outperform input-dependent routing on average. To examine when and how much specialization helps, we introduce GalaxyTS, a controlled synthetic dataset with exact shared and channel-specific forecasting references. It reveals how persistent channel mixtures exploit predictive differences concealed by short input windows and measures gains over matched shared corrections. These insights motivate Persistent Closed-Form Routing (PCR), a plug-and-play method that alternates exact conditional estimation of channel-specific mixture weights with gradient-based training of low-rank residual experts around a frozen pretrained forecaster. Averaged over four forecasting horizons, PCR-K4 achieves dataset-balanced mean squared error reductions of 3.86-14.25% relative to the three frozen backbones. In matched comparisons, PCR outperforms competing specialization methods on average while requiring substantially fewer trainable parameters.

Machine Learning.title: Memory or a Clock? Auditing a Memory Advantage in XLand-MiniGrid with Seeds, Maps and Evaluation Noise Apart
Machine Learning.summary: On a partially observable XLand-MiniGrid task, an LSTM agent beats a memory-free MLP by 25 percentage points. The gap looks like a clear case of memory. We ask two questions about it. First, how much of a measured gap is noise? Separating training seed, map and evaluation randomness in 60 runs, each re-evaluated three times, we find that about ten paired seeds detect a 10-point gap in final success. The binary "task acquired" verdict, a common summary of learning curves, is 76% evaluation noise and would need about a hundred seeds for the same gap. Second, is the gap memory? On a sealed panel of new maps, opened once, a memory-free MLP of the LSTM's size comes within 3.3 points of the LSTM when it is given the time step, and gains no measurable benefit from its width without it. With the time step, an MLP a quarter of the LSTM's size, and the LSTM with its state erased at every step, also come within about 5 points. A linear probe reads the time step from the trained LSTM's state. On this task, most of the apparent memory advantage is an advantage of knowing the time, which matters because episodes are cut at a fixed limit and the reward shrinks with time. We recommend giving memory-free baselines the time step, and we release the protocol, the event-driven tooling and every checkpoint.
Machine Learning.comment: 17 pages, 7 figures. Code: https://github.com/Effiani-Core/memory-or-clock . Data and checkpoints: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23512311

Machine Learning.title: Rectified Language Flow
Machine Learning.summary: Continuous-state flow and diffusion models offer a promising approach to fast, parallel language generation, but matching the generation quality of autoregressive models remains challenging. We present Rectified Language Flow (ReLF), a language model that generates text by transporting noise to token embeddings using rectified flow. ReLF combines several complementary design choices: fixed token embeddings constructed with Hellinger-SVD, self-conditioning guidance trained with cross-entropy, and regularized reflow for few-step generation. We further introduce singular logits, which combine an analytically computed term that drives commitment to a valid token embedding as noise vanishes with a bounded neural residual that learns contextual token preferences. With 64 function evaluations on OpenWebText, ReLF achieves lower generative perplexity than autoregressive baselines at matched diversity across all three model sizes tested, while also outperforming prior continuous flow methods in this setting. After two reflow rounds, ReLF still outperforms autoregressive baselines with 16 function evaluations while generating 1,024-token sequences 15-19 times faster at batch size 1.

Machine Learning.title: ProMo3D: Probing Motion Cues in Frozen 3D Foundation Models
Machine Learning.summary: Feed-forward 3D foundation models have recently reshaped multi-view reconstruction, yet dynamic 4D understanding still often relies on large-scale motion supervision or hand-crafted, architecture-specific heuristics. We ask whether frozen 3D foundation model tokens already encode motion-relevant information that can be exposed by lightweight readout functions, rather than re-learning motion-specific features with high-capacity decoders. Through probing on three representative backbones, we find that static--dynamic separation is decodable from frozen token representations. Our rank-restricted and spectral analyses on $π^3$X reveal that the recovered motion cues are concentrated in a low-dimensional subspace. Building on this, we propose Probing-based Motion Distillation (PMD), which converts pairwise motion-state compatibility scores against a fixed anchor token into dense motion masks. Trained on only 160 YouTube-VOS videos using a single 16 GB GPU, PMD transfers zero-shot to DAVIS, SegTrackv2, and FBMS-59 without target-benchmark fine-tuning. With multi-view pretrained geometric backbones, PMD outperforms training-free heuristics and approaches substantially heavier supervised and self-supervised methods, suggesting that motion decoding from frozen 3D foundation models can be lightweight and data-efficient.

Machine Learning.title: One Scan is Enough: Demonstration-Free Adaptation for Language-Guided Navigation
Machine Learning.summary: Deploying a language-guided navigation policy in a new building usually means watching it fail. Public-benchmark VLAs degrade scene by scene as layout, appearance, and language drift, and the standard fix of teleoperating fresh trajectories on site does not scale. We replace human demonstration with a single brief iPhone scan. Scan2Instruction compiles that scan into a complete training environment, automatically synthesizing executable navigation episodes with grounded instructions. PRPT-KS then adapts the policy through a closed-form Pareto utility read directly off the reconstructed scene, with no learned critic and no human labels. Across five real environments, the two designs together drive our RealNav to an 85% real-robot success rate, compared with 49% for a RealNav baseline post-trained on human demonstrations, and still achieve 82% in unscanned regions of the same buildings, compared with 41% for the same baseline. Our work turns demonstration-free scene adaptation for language-guided navigation from an aspiration into a working reality.

Machine Learning.title: Unlocking the Specialization Capability of PPG Foundation Models for Wearable Signals through Structured Pruning and Adaptive Fine-Tuning
Machine Learning.summary: Photoplethysmography (PPG) plays a central role in wearable health monitoring and clinical decision support. However, existing approaches to universal PPG representation learning are predominantly trained on high-quality large-scale datasets obtained from oximeters in hospital settings and often struggle to adapt to sparse and low-quality real-world datasets, thereby limiting their generalization to clinically relevant tasks on prevalent PPG data such as collected from wearable devices. Surprisingly, even after full fine-tuning, PPG foundation models cannot consistently outperform general-purpose time-series models. Therefore, a key question is how to effectively adapt PPG foundation models to target prediction tasks. Through empirical studies on various PPG foundation models, we find that pretrained models often exhibit inherent sparsity and computational redundancy, suggesting that PPG foundation models have learned to activate task-relevant network substructures for different prediction tasks. To preserve this valuable prior knowledge, we propose a structured pruning-and-fine-tuning framework, SPAFT, which regularizes the adaptive fine-tuning process by constraining it to a more relevant and compact parameter space based on parameter importance and structural redundancy. Extensive experiments across four PPG foundation models, five benchmark datasets, and ten downstream tasks demonstrate that SPAFT achieves win rates of 82.8% and 87.5% on regression and classification tasks, respectively. This prune-then-finetune paradigm often enables PPG foundation models to achieve state-of-the-art performance, laying a promising foundation for the real-world clinical deployment of PPG foundation models and the development of personalized PPG foundation models.

Machine Learning.title: Greedy Orthogonal Polynomial Manifolds with Lipschitz Control for Dimensionality Reduction and Reduced Modeling
Machine Learning.summary: Polynomial manifolds provide nonlinear low-dimensional representations through polynomial decoders. We propose to represent the polynomial terms of the decoder using features that are orthonormal on the training data. This empirical orthogonality enables a greedy algorithm, Greedy-OPM, which jointly selects encoder modes and polynomial features while minimizing the reconstruction error under a prescribed bound on the decoder's Lipschitz constant. Numerical experiments show that this Lipschitz constraint improves generalization away from the training data while retaining high reconstruction accuracy.

Machine Learning.title: Random-Bridges as Stochastic Transports for Generative Models
Machine Learning.summary: This paper motivates the use of random-bridges -- stochastic processes conditioned to take target distributions at fixed timepoints -- in the realm of generative modelling. Herein, random-bridges act as stochastic transports between two probability distributions when appropriately initialized, displaying either Markovian or non-Markovian, and continuous, discontinuous, or hybrid patterns depending on the choice of the driving process. We show how one can start from general probabilistic statements and branch out into specific representations for learning and simulation algorithms. Essentially, our framework formulates stochastic transports as noisy information processes governing the dynamic translation and propagation of information between arbitrary probability measures. Our theoretical and algorithmic presentation details training and simulation frameworks for both Gaussian and Lévy (specifically, Gamma, Poisson and Stable-$1/2$) random-bridge transports. The empirical validation focuses on the Gaussian case for demonstration and comparison purposes, where our construct delivers high-quality samples, achieving competitive Fréchet Inception Distance scores compared to widely used denoising diffusions and flow matching frameworks.

Machine Learning.title: The Geometry of Limits in ReLU Function Spaces
Machine Learning.summary: We study the geometry and closure of spaces of functions realized by ReLU neural networks of fixed architecture. We first establish a general result about limits of continuous piecewise-linear (CPWL) functions: the minimum number of convex sets on which a function is affine is lower semicontinuous under pointwise convergence. The proof uses a connection to hypergraph coloring and a compactness principle, and yields quantitative bounds on the polyhedral complexity of continuous limits. We then characterize the functions realizable by shallow ReLU networks with vector-valued outputs, extending a known scalar-valued characterization. Using this and the geometry of limiting hyperplane arrangements, we prove that fixed-width shallow scalar ReLU realization spaces are closed in the weighted supremum norm on the whole input space. In contrast, we construct an explicit sequence of networks with architecture $(2,3,2\mid1)$ whose limit is not realizable by that architecture. Non-closedness holds both globally in weighted supremum norm and under uniform convergence on compact sets with nonempty interior, disproving a conjecture of Petersen, Raslan, and Voigtlaender. Finally, we show that non-closedness for a fixed scalar-output ReLU architecture necessarily involves a \emph{blow-up residue}, in which diverging output coefficients amplify an emerging linear dependence among hidden features. Together, these results provide geometric and functional-analytic tools for studying the boundaries and degenerations of ReLU realization spaces.

Machine Learning.title: TriageRAG: Failure-Aware Self-Training for Adapting Retrieval-Augmented Language Models to Specialized Domains
Machine Learning.summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) lets large language models (LLMs) answer knowledge-intensive questions from retrieved evidence, but adapting a general-purpose RAG system to a specialized domain such as medicine is difficult when only an unlabeled corpus is available. Self-training approaches such as SimRAG address this by letting the LLM write its own question-answer pairs from domain passages and fine-tuning on the pairs that survive a round-trip consistency filter. We observe that these approaches treat every retained example identically: they never ask whether the student already knows the answer, already extracts it correctly from the retrieved context, or fails - and if so, whether the failure lies with the reader or with the retriever. To tackle this, we propose TriageRAG, a failure-aware self-training approach that probes the student on each self-generated question with and without retrieved context, triages it into one of four categories (known, solved, context-failure, retrieval-failure), and routes each category to the training signal that addresses it, including a parametric route that teaches the reader to answer when retrieval misses. Probing is cheap and repeated every round, so the training mixture follows the student, and the triage histogram doubles as a label-free diagnostic of where the domain gap lies. Experiments on 11 datasets spanning three domains with a Qwen3-4B backbone, and on CS-Bench with Qwen3-8B, demonstrate that TriageRAG outperforms a budget-matched SimRAG by 1.2-6.4 points and is the only method that recovers the closed-book level in every case where retrieval hurts the base model. A single ablation identifies the mechanism: round-trip filtering removes every training context that lacks the evidence, and a reader that never sees such contexts learns to over-trust noisy retrieval.

Machine Learning.title: Efficient Linear Attention for Multivariate Time Series Modeling via Entropy Calibration
Machine Learning.summary: Attention mechanisms are effective for multivariate time series modeling because they adaptively aggregate information across timestamps and variables. Their quadratic cost, however, limits their use in multivariate and spatio-temporal systems. Linear attention reduces this cost by replacing nonlinear attention mappings with forms that support associative computation. Replacing exponential weighting may weaken the amplification of high-score positions and further bias weakly selective distributions toward uniform aggregation. We propose an entropy-calibrated linear attention module and instantiate it as the ELinFormer forecaster. Our operator decomposes aggregation into a uniform component and a query-dependent correction, whose magnitude is calibrated by a query-specific temperature. We derive a second-order KL proxy from centered query-key scores. The Taylor expansion reduces the proxy to the squared-score energy divided by the squared temperature. This score energy can be computed from shared products of the centered keys without forming the full pairwise score matrix, and the same products support the linear attention output. We design a smooth temperature rule to calibrate the KL proxy: it keeps low-energy residuals vanishing, approximately calibrates moderate-energy queries to a shared KL level, and allows the proxy to continue growing for high-energy queries. Experiments on five PEMS benchmarks show competitive forecasting accuracy. Controlled comparisons with vanilla attention and Linformer demonstrate a favorable accuracy--memory trade-off, while analysis on PEMS08 shows that the proposed rational temperature rule and query-specific calibration achieve lower MAE than a linear rule or shared-temperature alternatives. These results support entropy calibration as an effective mechanism for preserving selective deviations in linear attention.
Machine Learning.comment: 10-page main paper with a 6-page supplement, 4 figures in total. Version 2 revises the theoretical formulation and proofs, adds a high-energy interpretation and controlled NaLaFormer comparison, and expands reproducibility material, and the core method is unchanged. Code on https://github.com/LenarBe/ElinFormer

Machine Learning.title: An actively trained neural operator for near-explicit atmospheric chemistry
Machine Learning.summary: Earth-system models simplify atmospheric chemistry into condensed mechanisms, because near-explicit mechanisms such as the Master Chemical Mechanism (MCM) are too costly to solve in every grid cell. Neural emulators could lift this limit, but most advance the chemistry in small time steps and cover only a few species or a reduced mechanism. Here we introduce FNO-MoE, a Fourier neural operator with a mixture of experts that predicts the full near-explicit chemical state over 30 minutes in a single call. The same network also guides its own training, using the disagreement among its experts to select the most informative box-model simulations. At equal cost, this active sampling yields a more accurate emulator than random or evenly spread sampling. Fine-tuning on longer trajectories keeps it stable over multi-hour runs in which models trained on short simulations diverge. The resulting emulator reproduces the evolution of thousands of species with high fidelity, remains accurate for unseen chemical compositions and runs orders of magnitude faster than the numerical solver. These results open a new direction for emulating complex atmospheric systems: neural operators that predict the full chemical state over long windows and choose their own training data. Training under changing meteorology is the next step towards bringing near-explicit chemistry into Earth-system models.

Machine Learning.title: CFL-aware edge design for graph neural solvers of hyperbolic transport
Machine Learning.summary: Hyperbolic partial differential equations (PDEs) transport information at finite speed along characteristics, often producing shocks and discontinuities that are challenging to capture numerically. Graph neural networks (GNNs) offer learned update rules, but neighbor aggregation alone does not tell a GNN how far information must travel and along which edge. As a result, when a GNN model takes a time step larger than what was used in training, shock fronts smear and oscillations grow. In this work, we ask whether making the scale of transport explicit as an edge-local Courant-Friedrichs-Lewy (CFL) signal can enhance GNNs' ability to model hyperbolic PDEs. Holding the architecture fixed, we vary only the information given to each edge, from a raw edge form to forms that progressively expose the edge-local transport interaction through direction, length, and wave speed. Because all of these are computed from the same ingredients, what changes is not the amount of information but its form. The results show a consistent pattern, in which feature count is not the limiting factor, and appending CFL directly to a raw edge form produces almost no benefit. The CFL conditioning proves most effective when the edge information already exposes the transport interaction, reducing final-step error by 10.4-14.4%, and the improvement widens as the step size grows larger. Notably, this improvement arises not from smearing the solution but from suppressing oscillations near shocks. These results point to a specific design principle that CFL conditioning is most effective when the edge representation already separates the direction of interaction from spatial scale, so that the CFL value has a well-defined quantity to modulate.

Machine Learning.title: StateWise: Teaching Language Models to Track and Obey Evolving Constraints in Multi-Turn Dialogue
Machine Learning.summary: Users of conversational assistants rarely state all requirements up front: they add constraints, amend them, withdraw them, digress, and return. Instruction-tuned LLMs fail here in two ways: active constraints stop being honored as turns accumulate (persistence failure), and withdrawn constraints keep being enacted (relapse). The only existing repair we know of is an external ledger that re-injects a compiled specification every turn. We propose StateWise, a self-improving approach that teaches a single LLM to maintain its own revisable constraint state, a typed state with tombstones for revoked constraints, so persistence and relapse are measured by executable checkers and ground-truth states are compiled for free. StateWise fine-tunes the LLM on two complementary skills, summarizing a dialogue into its constraint state and responding conditioned on that state, then self-trains on its own trajectories, keeping only turns that pass an exact round-trip check against the compiled state. This teaches 7-8B models to track the state almost perfectly but, surprisingly, not to obey it: on Llama-3.1-8B every supervised variant roughly doubles relapse. We therefore add a preference stage on self-generated relapse contrasts, where the rejected response enacts a revoked rule and the chosen one passes the round-trip check. On two backbones with held-out constraint families and unseen phrasings, StateWise cuts relapse by 8-22 points relative to supervised self-training, lifts conversation success by 8-19 points over the backbone, and beats an oracle compiled-ledger baseline on relapse with no inference-time scaffolding. We also characterize the recipe's cost on general instruction-following benchmarks and study weight interpolation as a mitigation.

Machine Learning.title: Gefen: Optimized Stochastic Optimizer
Machine Learning.summary: AdamW is a default optimizer for deep learning, but its moment states add two parameter-sized buffers to training memory, increasing the cost of large-scale pretraining. We propose Gefen, a memory-efficient optimizer that automatically shares second-moment estimates across parameter blocks and quantizes the first moment using a learned codebook. Gefen reduces AdamW's optimizer memory footprint by up to 8x while maintaining performance, saving 6.5 GiB per billion parameters. Prior work shares second moments across parameters grouped along the Hessian's block-diagonal structure, but relies on hand-specified architectural rules and leaves unexplained why such grouping works. We prove that large mixed Hessian entries constrain the ratio of squared gradients toward one, explaining why shared second moments are accurate when the squared gradients they pool are similar. The Hessian need not be computed: its block structure is inherited by squared gradients, allowing blocks to be found directly. Gefen therefore infers block structure from initial squared gradients, requiring no architecture-specific metadata or user-tuned hyperparameters beyond AdamW defaults. Gefen learns an exact histogram-based dynamic-programming quantization codebook and reuses the blocks for first-moment scaling. Across diverse pretraining experiments, Gefen achieves the lowest peak optimizer memory among compared methods that maintain AdamW-level performance. In single-machine and distributed training, the reduced footprint enables larger microbatches and substantially improves throughput over AdamW, making Gefen a drop-in replacement that can train larger models or use larger global batch sizes. We provide the complete Python implementation, including fused CUDA kernels at https://github.com/ndvbd/Gefen

Machine Learning.title: Bias-Aware Adjoint Calibration and Optimal Control of Stochastic Multiscale Bioprocess Digital Twins
Machine Learning.summary: We develop a bias-aware digital-twin calibration and control framework for multiscale bioprocess models within a biological systems-of-systems (Bio-SoS) paradigm. The digital twin is represented by a stochastic differential equation (SDE) model and calibrated from sparse observations using quasi-likelihood estimation and adjoint sensitivity analysis. SDE generator-based moment expansions characterize truncation-induced parameter bias, while forward-backward adjoints quantify how calibration uncertainty propagates to value functions and policy performance. The resulting parameter-error distribution supports both policy-directed data acquisition and uncertainty-aware policy optimization through a second-order Gaussian-averaged objective. We characterize the asymptotic behavior of the resulting exploration criterion and derive a physical-system performance under the optimized policy. To implement these ideas, we develop an Actor-Simulator algorithm that jointly updates model parameters, selects informative experiments, and optimizes control policies. Numerical studies demonstrate improved calibration accuracy, sample efficiency, and control performance relative to state-of-the-art baselines.

Machine Learning.title: Diagonally-Weighted Generalized Method of Moments Estimation for Gaussian Mixture Modeling
Machine Learning.summary: With direct computation of moments through order $L$ in $d$ dimensions, standard method of moments (MM) incurs $Ω(d^L)$ computation and storage costs, and standard generalized method of moments (GMM) additionally requires estimating and inverting an often ill-conditioned covariance matrix of size $Ω(d^L)$-by-$Ω(d^L)$ to obtain the optimal weighting matrix. Pereira, Kileel, and Kolda [arXiv:2202.06930 (2022)] avoid the tensor computation cost of MM through implicit moment computation. Despite this progress, incorporating statistically principled weighting while preserving computational efficiency remains an important challenge, particularly at low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), where sampling variances can differ substantially across moment orders. We introduce diagonally-weighted GMM (DGMM), which assigns one adaptive weight to each moment order through a structured approximation of the optimal weighting matrix while avoiding the covariance inversion, thereby balancing statistical efficiency, computational complexity, and numerical stability. For general parametric models, we prove that DGMM is consistent, asymptotically normal, and near-efficient under explicit structural conditions. For heteroscedastic low-rank Gaussian mixtures, we design a computationally efficient and numerically stable algorithm that extends the implicit moment computation to the DGMM objective, gradients, and weights and incorporates Nyström approximations of the kernel sums. In low-SNR experiments with $d=100$ and $L=4$, where standard MM and GMM are infeasible, controlled weighting comparisons show that DGMM achieves consistently small parameter errors across tested initializations, including the challenging starts where alternative weightings struggle, with shorter median runtimes and fewer iterations. The code and data will be available upon publication at https://github.com/liu-lzhang/dgmm.

Machine Learning.title: A Distribution-Matching Perspective on LLM Training Algorithms
Machine Learning.summary: In this work, we propose a unified framework for training algorithms across different stages of modern large language model development, based on the perspective of distribution matching. We show that a broad class of language model training algorithms can be interpreted as minimizing a certain divergence between the current model and a target distribution, and that characterizing the properties of this target distribution provides substantial insight into the behavior of the corresponding training algorithms. By analyzing specific forms of the target distribution, we establish that On-Policy Distillation (OPD) enjoys an advantage over classical Knowledge Distillation (KD) when the current model distribution is close to the target distribution, while exhibiting a disadvantage when the two distributions are far apart. Furthermore, when the target distribution itself depends on the model being optimized, we show that the accumulation of estimation variance can induce a deterministic degradation of the target distribution. These results provide a theoretical explanation, at least in part, for the long-term behavior of existing Reinforcement Learning (RL) algorithms. With this intuition we further designed Conditional KL (CKL) regularization for mitigating the degradation of the target distribution. CKL can effectively preserve mode diversity while relaxing the constraint imposed by classical KL regularization on reward improvements. We believe this theoretical perspective can bring some new understanding of language model training algorithms and provide useful guidance for future research.

Machine Learning.title: A quantum k-nearest neighbors implementation using magnitude-aware comparisons
Machine Learning.summary: Much attention has recently been devoted to the k-nearest neighbors (KNN) algorithm as a case study for quantum computing algorithms. Several algorithms have devised methods to compute a similarity metric to solve Quantum KNN (QKNN). This paper presents a practical quantum encoding technique that enables Euclidean distance calculation between vectors with different L2 norms by appending a single component to each vector, then uses it in the QKNN problem. It is arguably simpler to understand and implement than comparable methods and uses fewer qubits. Further, an implementation of this algorithm is provided and is used to benchmark it against a recent Euclidean-distance QKNN method on standard labeled datasets. In addition to demonstrating proper formulation, the results show marked improvement over similar implementations during simulation with realistic noise due to the use of fewer qubits and thus more coherent circuits.

Machine Learning.title: Polynomial Residual Networks are Generically Identifiable
Machine Learning.summary: We prove identifiability results for constant-width residual networks with polynomial activations and bias terms. For activations of degree at least five with generic coefficients, the fiber over a generic parameter is a singleton. For activations of degree at least three with no linear term after a suitable translation of the input, the generic fiber is given by translating biases and then scaling weights and translated biases by real roots of unity. These results specialize to networks without bias terms. With the same proof technique, we further derive necessary conditions for critical points of the ResNet parametrization, that are central in singular learning theory.

Machine Learning.title: A SegFormer-based model for spatial Daylight Factor prediction with comprehensive obstruction encoding and regulatory validation
Machine Learning.summary: Daylight compliance assessment in residential buildings requires time-consuming raytracing simulations and specialist model preparation, limiting its integration into iterative architectural design. We present a machine learning-based methodology for predicting the spatial distribution of the Daylight Factor (DF) directly within Building Information Modelling (BIM) environments, delivering results in seconds without model export or manual curation. The approach addresses five gaps not jointly covered by any existing model: external obstruction encoding including balconies, own building height, variable material reflectances, non-orthogonal room geometries, and regulatory validation. Two models are developed: a default-materials model with fixed reflectances for preliminary design checks, and a custom-materials model with variable project-specific reflectances. Both are trained on about 20,000 synthetic Radiance-simulated rooms and validated on a held-out synthetic dataset and 102 rooms from 18 real building models. The default-materials model achieves $δ_1$ = 83.4% and MAE = 0.11% DF on synthetic data, and on real buildings predicts BBR (Swedish) compliance area within 4.85 pp MAE (bias +2.31 pp) and TEK17 (Norwegian) mean room DF within 0.304% DF MAE (bias +0.287% DF). The custom-materials variant shows 1.7-2.4$\times$ higher error across all metrics. Both models concentrate accuracy in the BBR compliance-critical zone (DF < 1%), achieving a sub-1% DF MAE of 0.105% DF and Compliance IoU of 0.883 on real buildings. All cases where compliance is overestimated are borderline, within 10.7 pp of the BBR threshold (median 3.2 pp) and 0.36% DF of the TEK17 threshold (median 0.10% DF). The default-materials model is recommended as a replacement for preliminary daylight simulations; the custom-materials variant requires further development before use in final compliance verification.
Machine Learning.comment: Conference: BuildSim Nordic 2026 15 pages, Appendices A, B, C 9 figures, 8 tables

Machine Learning.title: Trust Mechanisms for Offline Generative AI at the Edge: A Connectivity-Regime Framework and an Empirical Study on a Raspberry Pi 5
Machine Learning.summary: Generative AI and large language models (LLMs) are moving into the Internet of Things, yet most deployments assume cloud connectivity, and many IoT settings have intermittent, restricted, or no connectivity. We propose a connectivity-regime framework (C0-C4), a taxonomy of inference-time trust mechanisms, and signed, versioned knowledge packs as the update channel for disconnected regimes, and evaluate them on a Raspberry Pi 5 running fully local retrieval-augmented generation under network isolation, with three Qwen2.5 model sizes, three context sizes, and 300 SQuAD 2.0 questions. An empirically calibrated retrieval-score gate detects knowledge gaps almost perfectly (AUROC 0.97) but in-topic unanswerable questions poorly (0.68). A deterministic output validator converts malformed outputs into explicit abstentions with no observed loss of correct answers, while the NLI-based verifier we tested adds little; for the 7B model, 96% of substantive answers to unanswerable-labelled questions match normalized spans of the retrieved passages. A 3B model achieves the same gold-answer containment rate as a 7B model at less than half the latency and estimated energy, although the 7B model far more often exceeds a token-F1 threshold of 0.5; five retrieved passages lower correctness from 75% to 52% compared with three. Verifying a signed pack takes about 4.5 ms versus about 29 min for embedding its passages on the device; signature and hash checks alone accept six of nine tested update attacks that layered verification rejects. Yet a validly signed poisoned pack passes every pack check: on 30 previously correct questions, correct answers drop to zero and 14 return the injected answer. None of the mechanisms we evaluated establishes the truth of the evidence. We release code and data.
Machine Learning.comment: 25 pages, 4 figures, 6 tables. Code and data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23620709

Machine Learning.title: How Geometry Shapes Generative Model Evaluation on Riemannian Manifolds
Machine Learning.summary: On Riemannian manifolds, generative-model evaluation is geometry-dependent since curvature and dimension jointly determine distances and volume growth. Our framework systematically compares geodesic, ambient, and tangent-space versions of Wasserstein and MMD across different geometries. Using controlled-noise perturbations and Riemannian Flow Matching samples, we study metric agreement, noise sensitivity, and their relation to geometry-induced volume scaling. We find that no metric is uniformly reliable: evaluation distance can affect both measured discrepancies and noise sensitivity, varying across curvature and dimension. Our analysis leads to practical recommendations for reporting evaluation distances, comparing metric types, and calibrating metrics to the geometry of the samples.
Machine Learning.comment: NeurIPS 2026, Geometric Distributional Deep Learning workshop

Machine Learning.title: Learning Representative Port Subsets for Efficient Fluid Antenna Systems
Machine Learning.summary: Fluid antenna systems (FASs) provide many candidate ports, but probing all ports for each channel realization incurs substantial online overhead. We study a complementary offline problem: compress the candidate-port space once and reuse the compressed set across future channel realizations. The method collects optimal ports from sampled training realizations, requiring only one scan of the candidate ports per realization. On a DeepMIMO 7-by-7 FAS with 49 candidate ports, 120 training realizations yield 27 representative ports on average while retaining 99.995% of the channel power gain achieved by exhaustive port selection.

Machine Learning.title: Latent dynamics for reconstructing fine-scale PDE trajectories from coarse observations
Machine Learning.summary: Coarse PDE observations omit spatial detail and intermediate states of evolving fields. We present Structured Latent Dynamics (SLD), a framework that reconstructs high-resolution trajectories from spatially and temporally downsampled simulations. SLD interpolates the input in time, adds a learned temporal correction and uses the resulting sequence to guide a hidden state on the coarse grid. Each update of the latent state combines a learned gated response with horizontal and vertical central differences and a five-point Laplacian of the state. The three spatial terms have learned channel-wise coefficients. Two Haar wavelet synthesis branches map the hidden state and refined coarse input to the high-resolution field. We evaluate SLD on two-dimensional Gray--Scott, complex Ginzburg--Landau and viscous Burgers systems, reconstructing 100 output frames from 25 input frames with eightfold refinement in each spatial direction. SLD achieves lower mean relative $L_2$ error and mean absolute error than unstructured latent dynamics and ConvLSTM baselines with comparable parameter counts, both on held-out trajectories and on later windows of trajectories used during training. SLD also reduces errors in regions with large reference gradients and across most or all of the evaluated later time intervals. A representative Gray--Scott comparison shows lower spectral error over most intermediate and high wavenumbers. Removing the fixed spatial response increased reconstruction error, supporting its contribution to the SLD architecture.

Machine Learning.title: Lumbermark: Resistant Clustering by Chopping Up Mutual Reachability Minimum Spanning Trees
Machine Learning.summary: We introduce Lumbermark, a robust divisive clustering algorithm capable of detecting clusters of varying sizes, densities, and shapes. Lumbermark iteratively chops off large limbs connected by protruding segments of a dataset's mutual reachability minimum spanning tree. The use of mutual reachability distances smoothens the data distribution and decreases the influence of low-density objects, such as noise points between clusters or outliers at their peripheries. The algorithm can be viewed as a divisive version of Genie and an alternative to HDBSCAN that produces partitions with user-specified sizes. A fast, easy-to-use implementation of this new method is available in the open-source lumbermark package for Python and R. We show that Lumbermark performs well on benchmark data and hope it will prove useful to data scientists and practitioners across different fields.

Machine Learning.title: RoboJev: An Open Vision-Language Judge for Robot Success Detection
Machine Learning.summary: Many robot manipulation videos do not indicate whether the task was successfully completed. RoboJev-27B is an open-weight vision-language model that takes a task instruction, 10 frames of a manipulation attempt, and (if available) final frames from auxiliary cameras and predicts whether the robot accomplished the task. RoboJev-27B is a variant of JEV-27B-VL, trained with a rank-32 LoRA adapter on the language model only (keeping the vision encoder frozen) using 52,598 episode records. It also uses a source-specific KL penalty that applies only to research data, anchoring predictions closer to the original model on those sources. It uses a calibrated two-token readout that outputs success/failure probabilities in a single forward pass. On 268 held-out episodes of the same robot model (SO-101), RoboJev-27B attains 95.2% balanced accuracy and 0.993 AUROC. It also generalises to episodes collected by unseen labs/robots (AUROC = 0.890 over 459 episodes) as well as to clearly labelled community-collected episodes (accuracy = 93.3% over 135 episodes), where the base model attains an AUROC = 0.900 on the unseen-lab/robot subset with the same inputs. It takes 0.26 seconds per episode (median, serial) to infer on a single H100, which is about \$0.19 per 1,000 success predictions at \$2.69 per GPU-hour (not including media processing and serving costs). RoboJev-27B is released together with its inference code, along with a transparent evaluation: 20,628 predictions organized into 29 model/protocol entries are made available to facilitate browsing and to enable reproducible benchmarking of success detection. We also compare against strong API-based frontier VLMs, which take in fewer input frames (4 images from the primary camera only); note that this comparison is not strictly like-for-like because RoboJev-27B is given more frames at inference.
